clinicalPearls: A pericardial cyst is a benign, thin-walled, mesothelium-lined fluid-filled sac that usually does not communicate with the pericardial cavity, most often congenital in origin.
The classic location is the right cardiophrenic angle (roughly two-thirds of cases), with the left cardiophrenic angle next most common; atypical superior mediastinal locations occur but are rare.
Most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on chest radiography or cross-sectional imaging performed for another reason.

When symptomatic, patients may report atypical chest discomfort, dyspnoea or cough from local compression; serious complications such as compression of a cardiac chamber, rupture or infection are uncommon.
The typical 'spring-water' cyst contains clear serous fluid; the term reflects the classic clear appearance of aspirated contents.
CT shows a well-defined, non-enhancing, homogeneous water-attenuation lesion abutting the pericardium; MRI demonstrates low T1 and high T2 signal without contrast enhancement of the contents.
Asymptomatic, radiologically characteristic cysts can generally be managed conservatively with periodic imaging surveillance rather than intervention.
Intervention (percutaneous aspiration or, more definitively, surgical/thoracoscopic excision) is reserved for symptomatic, enlarging, complicated or diagnostically uncertain lesions.
reference.pathophysiology: Pericardial cysts are thought to arise from aberrant embryological development of the pericardial coelom, in which one of the mesenchymal lacunae that normally coalesce to form the pericardial sac fails to fuse and instead persists as an isolated, mesothelium-lined cavity. The resulting cyst has a thin fibrous wall lined by a single layer of mesothelial cells and typically contains clear serous fluid. Because it usually does not communicate with the pericardial space, it enlarges slowly by fluid secretion and is generally of little haemodynamic consequence. Rarely, acquired cysts follow inflammation, cardiac surgery or trauma. Mass effect, when it occurs, results from mechanical compression of adjacent structures rather than any intrinsic secretory or malignant behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: prominent epicardial or mediastinal fat pad
cystic mediastinal teratoma or other mediastinal mass
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax (water attenuation, non-enhancing, well-circumscribed)
cardiac or thoracic MRI (low T1, high T2 signal, no enhancement)
transthoracic echocardiography (echo-free space adjacent to the heart)
fluid analysis if aspirated (clear serous, benign mesothelial cells)
PET imaging in selected cases to exclude a metabolically active/malignant mass
interval imaging surveillance to document stability
redFlags: rapid enlargement or interval change on serial imaging
haemodynamic compromise or arrhythmia from cardiac chamber compression
features suggesting infection of the cyst (fever, wall enhancement, surrounding inflammation)
imaging characteristics atypical for a simple cyst (thick or enhancing wall, solid components, septations)
acute chest pain with sudden change in cyst size suggesting rupture
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; most pericardial cysts are benign, remain stable and never cause symptoms, and complete surgical excision when required is generally curative with a low recurrence rate.
pitfalls: Mistaking a loculated pericardial effusion or a solid/malignant mediastinal mass for a simple benign cyst without cross-sectional confirmation.
Proceeding to surgery for an incidental, asymptomatic, radiologically classic cyst that could be safely observed.
Overlooking rare but important complications such as compression, infection or spontaneous rupture in a symptomatic patient.
Relying on percutaneous aspiration alone, after which recurrence is common because the secretory lining remains.
Failing to consider a Morgagni hernia, which can mimic a right cardiophrenic-angle cyst.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases
Feigin DS et al. Pericardial cysts, Radiology
management: Manage asymptomatic, incidentally discovered cysts conservatively with reassurance, as most remain stable and benign
Reserve intervention for symptomatic cysts causing atypical chest discomfort, dyspnoea or cough, or for compression of an adjacent cardiac chamber or airway
Offer image-guided percutaneous aspiration of the clear serous cyst fluid as a less invasive option, accepting a risk of recurrence
Undertake complete surgical excision (thoracoscopic or open) for symptomatic, enlarging, complicated (rupture or infection) or diagnostically uncertain cysts, which is generally curative
Monitor conservatively managed cysts with serial cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) or echocardiography to detect enlargement or complications
Involve cardiothoracic surgery and use PET imaging when a metabolically active or malignant mass cannot be excluded
